summary: Divide a quantity in a given ratio using the find-one-part routine: total parts = sum of ALL ratio numbers; one part = quantity ÷ total parts; each share = its ratio number × one part. The guidance generalises this to three-part ratios (divide 180 in 1:2:3 = 6 parts, not 3) and works both directions: express a completed division back as a simplest-form ratio (10 and 14 → 5:7) and state a share as a fraction of the whole. The persistent hazard is using one part, rather than the sum of parts, as the denominator; a bar/tape model with the correct number of equal segments keeps the correct total visible as a check.
misconceptions: Dividing by a single part rather than the sum of parts (÷3 or ÷5 instead of ÷8), or in a 3-part ratio forgetting to include every part in the total.
Sharing the quantity equally among the number of terms (180 into three equal 60s for 1:2:3).
When reversing, writing the shares as a ratio without simplifying (10:14 left un-reduced), or reversing the order.
Confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole — stating a share as a/b of the whole rather than a/(a+b).

activities.title: Ratio-divider on a tape diagram (forward direction)
steps: Enter a ratio such as 1:2:3 and cut the strip into the SUM of the parts — six equal segments for 1:2:3, not three.
Let the quantity (e.g. 180) distribute across the equal segments and read off one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30.
Colour 1, 2 and 3 adjacent segments to read the shares 30, 60 and 90, then add them to check they return 180.
Repeat with a two-part ratio (e.g. share £60 in 2:3: 5 parts, one part = 12, shares 24 and 36, summing to 60).
activities.insight: A three-part ratio 1:2:3 needs six equal parts, not three; dividing once by the total number of parts and then scaling each term is the whole routine, and the shares must add back to the original quantity.

activities.title: Reverse station: write shares as a simplest-form ratio
steps: Take two actual shares (e.g. 24 sweets shared as 10 and 14) and write them as a ratio 10:14.
Simplify by dividing both terms by their highest common factor (÷2) to reach 5:7, keeping the order matching the shares as stated.
Explain how this is like simplifying a fraction, and check you have not reversed the order (14:10 is wrong for 10 then 14).
activities.insight: A completed division can be expressed back as a ratio, and a ratio must be reduced to simplest form by dividing by the common factor — directly analogous to simplifying a fraction.

activities.title: Part of the whole as a fraction
steps: For 1:2:3, state what fraction of the whole each share is: 1/6, 2/6 (=1/3) and 3/6 (=1/2), using the TOTAL of 6 parts as the denominator.
Contrast part-to-part with part-to-whole explicitly: the middle share is 2 parts out of 6 total, so 2/6, NOT 2/3.
Optionally toggle a colour band to light each part and reveal its fraction of the whole.
activities.insight: When stating a share as a fraction of the whole, the denominator is the SUM of all parts (a+b+c), not another single term; part-to-part and part-to-whole use the same numbers differently.

activities.title: Checks for understanding (written/selected response)
steps: Fill in: divide 180 in 1:2:3 → __, __, __ (answer 30, 60, 90; the equal-share response 60, 60, 60 is a common error).
Choose the simplest-form ratio for shares of 10 and 14 (answer 5:7; the un-simplified 10:14 is a distractor).
State what fraction of the whole the middle share of 1:2:3 is (answer 2/6 = 1/3).
activities.insight: Three-part division, reverse-to-ratio, and part-of-whole can each be checked, with 'shared equally' and 'un-simplified ratio' as the diagnostic error responses; add a two-part item (e.g. £60 in 2:3) if two-part division is also to be checked.

checkQuestion: Divide 180 in the ratio 1:2:3. Work out the three amounts, and show your working. Then, separately: 24 sweets were shared as 10 and 14 — write that sharing as a ratio in its simplest form.
checkAnswer: For 180 in 1:2:3: total parts = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, so one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30; the shares are 30, 60 and 90 (which add to 180). For the reverse: 10:14 simplifies (÷2) to 5:7.
